narration: You see a sale tag — 'was $199, now just $97.' Your brain says deal. But here's the thing: that original price was never real.
visual: Large sale tag SVG with crossed-out $199 and '$97 NOW', excited person silhouette below, 'NEVER REAL' badge springs in at end. Dark background, orange accent.

narration: Retailers call it reference pricing. They set a high fake anchor, almost never sell at it, then slash it — so you feel like you're winning. You're not.
visual: Three-step flowchart on light background: Step 1 set $199 (0 units sold), Step 2 mark as $97 sale, Step 3 profit. 'LEGAL. EVERYWHERE.' badge springs in.

narration: The FTC investigated and found 85% of reference prices were never actually charged. Amazon settled a class action over this exact practice in 2022.
visual: Gavel SVG dropping from top, legal document card with FTC findings text, 85% stat badge springs in. Dark background.

narration: Here's why it works. Once your brain sees a number — even a fake one — it anchors to it. Then $97 feels tiny next to $199. That's the trap.
visual: Brain SVG springs in, two animated horizontal comparison bars: $199 full-width gray vs $97 half-width orange. 'YOUR BRAIN IS HACKED' badge. Light background.

narration: Consumer research puts the average annual cost at $2,600 — across clothing, electronics, and home goods. That 'deal' feeling is costing you thousands.
visual: Three shopping bags (clothing with shirt, electronics with laptop, home with house) rise from bottom one by one. Counter counts up to $2,600. Dark background.

narration: Before you buy, look up the item's actual price history. If that original price was never real — walk away. Follow for more tricks stores use to drain your wallet.
visual: Phone SVG with price history chart showing fake inflated reference dotted line vs real price orange line. Two green-check tips. Orange CTA badge. Light background.
